# Fitted Values and Residuals

## Decomposing an Observation Into Fitted Value and Residual

**The goal of this section:** separate what the line accounts for from what it
does not, one person at a time.

For each person the line produces a **fitted value**, and what is left over is
their **residual**.

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
y_i = \hat{y}_i + \hat{u}_i
\end{equation}
```

- $y_i$: what person $i$ actually earns
- $\hat{y}_i$: what the fitted line says they earn
- $\hat{u}_i$: the difference between the two
- $\bar{y}$: the average of $y$ across the sample

::: {.caveat title="A residual is not an error"}
$u_i$ is the population's error and we never see it. $\hat{u}_i$ is a leftover
we computed. Same hat convention as last week, same reason.
:::

<!-- IDEA 1. 10-35 min. -->

# Sums of Squares

## Total Sum of Squares

**The goal of this section:** turn a person-by-person split into three formal
quantities, and show that two of them add to the third.

How much does earnings vary in this sample at all, before schooling is
mentioned?

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{TSS} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( y_i - \bar{y} \right)^2
\end{equation}
```

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/figures/2-2_tss.png}{Each segment runs from a person to the
sample mean. The total sum of squares adds up their squares.}
```

<!-- IDEA 2. 38-63 min. -->

## Explained Sum of Squares

How much of that variation does the fitted line reproduce?

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{ESS} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( \hat{y}_i - \bar{y} \right)^2
\end{equation}
```

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/figures/2-2_ess.png}{Now each segment runs from the line to the
mean. Where the line is flat, this contributes nothing.}
```

## Residual Sum of Squares

What is left over once the line has done its work?

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{RSS} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left( y_i - \hat{y}_i \right)^2
             = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \hat{u}_i^{\,2}
\end{equation}
```

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/figures/2-2_rss.png}{The same segments least squares made as
small as it could last week.}
```

::: {.tablenotes}
This is the quantity we minimised in 2.1. Goodness of fit and the choice of
line are the same arithmetic, asked twice.
:::

## The Identity Linking the Three Sums of Squares

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{TSS} = \mathrm{ESS} + \mathrm{RSS}
\end{equation}
```

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/figures/2-2_bars.png}{The three totals as bars. The first
is the height of the other two.}
```

## Defining R-Squared From the Sums of Squares

```{=latex}
\begin{equation}
R^2 = \frac{\mathrm{ESS}}{\mathrm{TSS}} = 1 - \frac{\mathrm{RSS}}{\mathrm{TSS}}
\end{equation}
```

::: {.result}
$R^2$ is the share of the variation in earnings that moves with schooling in
this sample. It lies between nought and one only because the identity above
holds, and that identity holds only because of the first-order condition you
derived in 2.1.
:::

## Vote: Which Model Has the Higher R-Squared?

Two regressions on the same people: earnings on schooling, and earnings on
schooling plus their height in centimetres.

::: {.tablenotes}
Vote, argue, vote again. Then: does your answer depend on whether height
matters?
:::

# What R-Squared Will Not Tell You

## A High R-Squared With a Negligible Effect

**The goal of this section:** stop a number that measures spread being read as
a verdict on the model.

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/figures/2-2_rsq-tight.png}{Almost all the variation is
accounted for, and the effect is worth six cent an hour.}
```

::: {.tablenotes}
Precise, and unimportant. If you chose between models on R-squared you would
pick this one.
:::

<!-- IDEA 3. 66-92 min. -->

## A Low R-Squared With an Important Effect

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/figures/2-2_rsq-loose.png}{Almost none of the variation
is accounted for, and the effect is worth nearly two euro an hour.}
```

::: {.tablenotes}
Noisy, and important. Most of what moves earnings is not schooling, which is
a fact about the world rather than a fault in the regression.
:::

## A High R-Squared With a Misspecified Functional Form

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/figures/2-2_rsq-curved.png}{Earnings rise to about
fifteen years and then fall. The straight line reports a positive slope
throughout.}
```

::: {.caveat}
This is the dangerous one, because nothing about the number tells you it is
happening. You have to look at the picture.
:::

## Measuring Fit on a Hold-Out Sample

```{=latex}
\figpair{../_shared/figures/2-2_fit-sample.png}{The 120 the line was fitted
on.}{../_shared/figures/2-2_fit-holdout.png}{120 more from the same
population, which the line has never seen.}
```

::: {.tablenotes}
We held a second sample back before fitting anything. Fit measured on the data
you chose the line with is a claim about that data. Checking it somewhere else
is a different and harder claim.
:::

## Vote: Would You Publish This Regression?

An $R^2$ of 0.04, a slope of 1.9 euro a year, and 20,000 observations.

::: {.tablenotes}
Vote, argue, vote again. Then: which of the three numbers did you use?
:::

## What Would Have To Be True?

::: {.caveat title="The standing question"}
What would have to be true for this number to mean what we just said it means?
And what is the plausible story where it isn't?
:::

[Candidate this week: a high R-squared is compatible with a useless
model, and a low one with an important effect. The number tells you about
spread, and you were asked about importance.]

<!-- 92-97 min. Same slot every week. They answer in pairs first, then
     you. Not that causation is hard in the abstract, but that THIS
     estimate rests on something nameable that may well be false. -->

## Summary: The Three Parts of Goodness of Fit

Today was three separate ideas, each doing one job:

::: {.contributions}
1. **Fitted Values and Residuals.** Every person splits into a fitted value and a residual.
2. **Sums of Squares.** The sums of squares add up, which is what makes R-squared a share.
3. **What R-Squared Will Not Tell You.** A share of variation is not a verdict on the model.
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
Next week: whether the line we fitted is any good as an estimate, which is a different question from whether it fits.
:::

## Derivation: Why the Sums of Squares Add Up

Show that the total sum of squares equals the explained plus the residual sum
of squares.

::: {.tablenotes}
Two steps and a fact. Write the deviation of $y_i$ from its mean as the sum of
two pieces, square it, and sum. The step that does the work is the cross
term: it vanishes, and it vanishes because of the first-order condition you
derived last week. That is the only reason R-squared behaves like a share.
:::

[Full derivation. Set as homework; worked solution published with the set.]
